Tubes were not complete circuits. They were merely components that were included in a circuit of two or more components. Vacuum tubes still have a role today as some high power applications are best made from tube components (such as magnetron tubes for microwave ovens) though there are up and coming solid state components aiming to replace them. Many semiconductor devices today do not use any silicon. There are many more semiconductor materials that are better suited for modern integrated circuit and other semiconductor device manufacturing such as Gallium Arsenide, Cadmium Selenide and fused quartz substrates. LEDs use these more exotic substrates like GaAs GaInP and GaAlInP because they allow for crystal formations that produce visible and invisible light output with relatively low power requirements.

As for tubes, a new variety of vacuum tube technology has come around in the last decade. The Japanese synthesizer manufacturer Korg teamed up with vacuum fluorescent display maker Noritake to produce the NuTube. The NuTube is a low power, small size vacuum tube equivalent that is made using the same processes as vacuum fluorescent displays. They can bring the warmth and smoothness that older vacuum tubes did to audio applications, hence Korg's interest in making the devices. They are also impervious to radiation which make them ideal for use in space applications which would destroy non-hardened semiconductor devices. Tubes are far from dead.

The core unit of a computer is a transistor. There are many types of transistors. An IC is a special configuration of transistors that are designed to do a specific calculation based on input.

An IC is the hardware equivilant of a software function. Input volts on pins, transistors react to those volts, then output volts on other pins.

Electrical engineer here. Integrated circuits (IC for short) are just as the name suggests- a complete circuit built into a single integrated package. The concept came from the early days of semiconductor technology where manufacturers such as Farichild and Texas Instruments were looking to integrate multiple transistors and other components into complete circuits that could be packaged into a small "outline". An outline is the term used to describe the physical packaging of a transistor, integrated circuit or other electronic component. Outline can take on many forms but today we mostly see outline packages that are very small and contains many electrical connection points. But I'm getting ahed of myself here.

The manufacture of an IC begins with a prepared wafer substrate. This substrate is a material, such as silicon, which is grown in a special crystal structure (epitaxial arrangement) and produced as a large ingot. The ingot is sawed into thin wafers and chemically cleaned and treated for grow an oxide layer on its surface. This prepared wafer is then treated chemically to apply a light sensitive layer similar to what is done in make silk screens. These now photosensitive wafers are exposed through a photographic like process using masks and a strong very short wavelength ultraviolet light (extreme UV or XUV for short) since most of the features on this mask are incredibly small when scaled down to the size of the IC. Once exposed, the photosensitive layer hardens. A chemical process strips away unhardened parts that were blocked from the XUV light by the mask. An acid wash etches away material that is not protected by the hardened mask material leaving behind channels. With the unexposed areas now cleaned away, a plasma vapor deposition method is used to apply other materials into the channels. These materials include P-doped or N-doped semiconductor material and metals to make electrical connections between features and layers. The newly filled wafer is then re-coated in a photosensitive film layer and a new mask is exposed on top of it. The acid again etches channels and materials are vapor deposited once more. This repeats for two or more layers building up 3D structures of doped semiconductor material. A stack of two or more doped layers is called a junction and controls the flow of electrons like a switch, resists the flow like a resistor or provides one way flow like a diode. Various other junctions are possible to perform special functions like current sources and voltage dividers. All of these junctions connected by metal pathways deposited as vaporized particles form a complete circuit that would normally be massive if made out of individual full sized components. This is one of the greatest benefits of ICs in that they shrink circuits down to minute scales.

Once a wafer of devices have been processed, testing occurs to determine which devices are functioning properly. Any bad or out of spec devices are marked for disposal or for use as lower grade components. A wafer sawing machine that uses fine wires cuts the wafer into strips and finally individual chips. A wafer can contain hundreds or thousands of copies of the chips making batch manufacturing easier. Chips that tested good are now ready for packaging in one of various outline styles. Some newer devices actually have no packaging and are intended to have the bare chip bonded directly to a circuit board. Others require a sealed package usually made of epoxy and containing a structure called a "lead frame". Lead (as in to lead not the metal) frames are the physical metal pins or contacts that will make both internal and external electrical connections possible. The lead frame has a place for the chip (die is another term for this) to be mounted in place and very thin wires are electrically welded between these leads and the contact points created on the chip die. These wires are referred to as "cat whiskers" but are incredibly tiny compared to an actual cat whisker. With the chip die mounted to a lead frame and wired up to the individual leads, pins or pads, the assembly is not ready to be molded into an epoxy shape. The assembly goes into an injection molding die and epoxy is molded around it and chemically, thermally or optically cured to hardness. The new device package is now ready for more testing in an automated test machine that makes sure the component performs as intended.

Once a device tests good, labeling the next stop. While ICs used to be labeled with ink via a pad printing process, modern devices are laser engraved with a fiber laser. The manufacturer brand, part number, date code and other information are laser etched onto the epoxy package and the device moves on to bulk packaging. In bulk packaging, devices are placed into several types of multi component packaging. Smaller devices may be placed into plastic strips with recesses in them and covered in a plastic film and spooled onto reels. This is called "tape reel" packaging and is designed for automated machines called "pick and place" machines to automatically retrieve and attach the individual devices to circuit boards during assembly. Other larger devices go onto "egg trays" or "egg grates" which are plastic forms that hold chips in specific positions and orientations to ease automated assembly processes. Other types may be added in a line to plastic sleeves, but this is older technology and rarely seen in modern manufacturing. No matter what their final packaging is, these ICs are sent off to parts suppliers and manufacturers for use in all manner of industrial, commercial and consumer goods.

The integrated circuit is perhaps one of the most important technological developments in history. It changed the nature of man and the world. For better or for worse, the IC has left an indelible mark on the past, present and future of man. The work of great men in the latter half of the 20th century paved the way for so many things they could not have conceived of at that time. Their work makes it possible to actually have a tiny, extremely low cost microprocessor inside a cheap plastic toy from China that costs less to include in that toy than the handful of standard components that would do the equivalent function, say flash an LED or make a sound. I have a question: Why are wafers circular?

I would think they would be square/rectangular in order to minimize waste.

Good question! The answer is because of the way the silicon crystal is grown. The Czochralski process involves pulling a silicon seed crystal at the end of a rotating rod from a crucible of molten silicon (or gallium arsenide). The rotation and slow pulling of the rod upwards allows the seed crystal to grow in diameter and length as the molten silicon crystallizes on the seed. The highly pure crystal ingot (sometimes called a boule) is then cooled and eventually cut into thin wafers using a diamond saw. Wafers often have a flat side on the circumference of the wafer. This is done for two reasons: 1. slicing off a flat from the ingot allows the ingot to stay put during wafer slicing and 2. allows the wafers to be oriented properly during each successive operation in the chip making process. Sure they could trim off more excess and make square wafers with a little more space efficiency, but circular seems to be a good enough method since it allows for unused borders where the Scara wafer handling robots (these guys) can safely grip them without destroying any chip features.
